rows.speaker: ابن عطية
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAṭiyya reads the plants as interwoven with one another because of the water; on this reading the preposition marks cause.
rows.anchor: وقال ابن عطية: وصلت فرقة النبات بقوله فاختلظ أي: اختلط النبات بعضه ببعض بسبب الماء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The alternative making water the subject of “mixed” and pausing there is syntactically weak; the pause breaks connected, eloquent speech into obscure, uninformative wording.
rows.anchor: لأنه تفكيك للكلام المتصل الصحيح المعنى، الفصيح اللفظ

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The named foods distinguish edible plants: people eat grains, fruits, and vegetables, while livestock eat grass and other pasture.
rows.anchor: بين أن المراد أحد القسمين بمن فقال: مما يأكل الناس، كالحبوب والثمار

rows.speaker: الحوفي
rows.claim: Al-Ḥūfī attaches min to ikhtalaṭa; Abū al-Baqāʾ instead makes the phrase a circumstantial modifier of the plants, which Abū Ḥayyān regards as the clearer parse, with an omitted copula.
rows.anchor: قال الحوفي: من متعلقة باختلط

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The temporal particle ḥattā requires a preceding action that continues; supply continued growth, or understand ikhtalaṭa as the plants remaining mixed with water.
rows.anchor: وحتى غاية، فيحتاج أن يكون الفعل الذي قبلها متطاولا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The adornment is supplied by the plants, including their grains, fruits, and flowers.
rows.anchor: بنباتها وما أودع فيه من الحبوب والثمار والأزهار،

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Wa-izzayyanat may repeat the idea of taking adornment, or add that the land deliberately adorned itself; attributing both actions to the land is a fine metaphor.
rows.anchor: وازينت ليفيد أنها قصدت التزيين

rows.speaker: قراء الجمهور
rows.claim: The common reading assimilates the t of underlying watazayyanat into z and adds a connecting hamza because assimilation leaves z unvocalized.
rows.anchor: وقرأ الجمهور: وازينت وأصله وتزينت، فأدغمت التاء في الزاي

rows.speaker: أبي وعبد الله وزيد بن علي والأعمش
rows.claim: These readers have the unassimilated form wa-tazayyanat on the tafaʿʿalat pattern.
rows.anchor: وقرأ أبي وعبد الله، وزيد بن علي، والأعمش: وتزينت على وزن تفعلت

rows.speaker: سعد بن أبي وقاص وأبو عبد الرحمن وابن يعمر والحسن والشعبي وأبو العالية وقتادة ونصر بن عاصم وابن هرمز وعيسى الثقفي
rows.claim: This group reads wa-azyanat on the afʿalat pattern, meaning its adornment appeared or came due; the preserved yāʾ is rare, with azānat the expected form.
rows.anchor: وقرأ سعد بن أبي وقاص، وأبو عبد الرحمن، وابن يعمر، والحسن، والشعبي، وأبو العالية،

rows.speaker: أبو عثمان النهدي
rows.claim: Abū ʿUthmān al-Nahdī is reported with an open hamza in an unusual ifʿaʾallat form.
rows.anchor: وقرأ أبو عثمان النهدي بهمزة مفتوحة بوزن افعألت

rows.speaker: ابن عطية
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAṭiyya calls the related group reading a dialect and cites poetry as evidence; the elders of ʿAwf b. Abī Jamīla have a reading with doubled n, which Ibn ʿAṭiyya identifies with Abū ʿUthmān’s.
rows.anchor: ونسب ابن عطية هذه القراءة لفرقة فقال: وقرأت فرقة وازيأنت وهي لغة منها

rows.speaker: فرقة
rows.claim: Another group reads wa-zāyanat, from an assimilated original watazāyanat.
rows.anchor: وقرأت فرقة: وازاينت، والأصل وتزاينت فأدغم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Here ẓann has its ordinary sense of judging one possibility more likely; the proposed sense “they became certain” is unsound.
rows.anchor: والظن هنا على بابه من ترجيح أحد الجائزين

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Being able to manage the land means being able to harvest its crop, benefit from it, and obtain its yield, made possible by healthy growth free from blight.
rows.anchor: ومعنى القدرة عليها التمكن من تحصيلها ومنفعتها ورفع غلتها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The pronoun in ahluhā refers to the land, with an omitted noun meaning its crop’s people; readings that make it refer to the yield or adornment are weak.
rows.anchor: والضمير في أهلها عائد على الأرض، وهو على حذف مضاف

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The answer to idhā is “Our command came”; the command may be wind, cold or hot winds, mice, locusts, or another destructive calamity.
rows.anchor: وجواب إذا قوله: أتاها أمرنا كالريح والصر والسموم

rows.speaker: قيل
rows.claim: An alternative takes “Our command came” to mean that God’s command to destroy the crop arrived.
rows.anchor: وقيل: أتاها أمرنا بإهلاكها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The night-or-day wording either leaves the time unstated though God knows it, or distributes events: some lands are struck at night, others by day.
rows.anchor: وأبهم في قوله: ليلا أو نهارا، وقد علم تعالى متى يأتيها أمره

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ḥaṣīd is a passive sense meaning harvested; Abū ʿUbayda glosses it as cut off. Calling blighted crops “harvested” is metaphorical, or an implicit simile for harvested grain.
rows.anchor: والحصيد: فعيل بمعنى مفعول أي: المحصود

rows.speaker: أبو عبيدة
rows.claim: Abū ʿUbayda explains ḥaṣīd as completely uprooted or cut off.
rows.anchor: وقال أبو عبيدة: الحصيد المستأصل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “As if it had not flourished yesterday” intensifies devastation: the land seems never to have existed or displayed its pleasing green abundance.
rows.anchor: مبالغة في التلف والهلاك حتى كأنها لم توجد قبل

rows.speaker: الحسن وقتادة
rows.claim: Ḥasan and Qatāda read the verb with masculine agreement; the antecedent may be the omitted crop or adornment, but Abū Ḥayyān prefers the harvested crop.
rows.anchor: وقرأ الحسن وقتادة: كأن لم يغن بالياء على التذكير

rows.speaker: مروان بن الحكم
rows.claim: Marwān b. al-Ḥakam reportedly read tataġannā with two tāʾs; al-Aʿshā’s verse supports taghannī from ġaniya, “to dwell.”
rows.anchor: وكان مروان بن الحكم يقرأ على المنبر: كأن لم تتغن بتاءين

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Abū Ḥayyān rejects al-Zamakhsharī’s equation of yesterday with any time or with “just now”: the phrase means it seemed not to have existed in past time, emphasizing its rapid disappearance.
rows.anchor: وليس الأمس عبارة عن مطلق الوقت، ولا هو مرادف كقوله: آنفا

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: A report about Ubayy’s codex adds that God would not destroy the land except for its people’s sins; another transmitted wording names God explicitly.
rows.anchor: وفي مصحف أبي: كأن لم تغن بالأمس، وما كنا لنهلكها إلا بذنوب أهلها

rows.speaker: أبو سلمة بن عبد الرحمن
rows.claim: Abū Salama reportedly read in Ubayy’s reading that the land was destroyed only for its people’s sins; Abū Ḥayyān says this should not be recited because it departs from the agreed codex script.
rows.anchor: وكان أبو سلمة بن عبد الرحمن يقرأ في قراءة أبي كأن لم تغن بالأمس، وما أهلكناها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The concluding promise to detail signs for reflective people means that, as God detailed them earlier, He will detail them in what follows.
rows.anchor: أي: مثل هذا التفصيل الذي فصلناه في الماضي، نفصل في المستقبل

rows.speaker: أبو الدرداء
rows.claim: Abū al-Dardāʾ reads yatadhakkarūn with dhāl in place of the common fāʾ.
rows.anchor: وقرأ أبو الدرداء: لقوم يتذكرون بالذال بدل الفاء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: After the fleeting worldly life and its calamities, God calls people to the abode of safety, identified as Paradise because its people are free from every harm.
rows.anchor: لما ذكر مثل الحياة الدنيا وما يؤول إليه من الفناء والاضمحلال

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “Abode of peace” may honor God by attributing the Garden to His name, or refer to safety and the inhabitants’ mutual and angelic greetings of peace.
rows.anchor: ويجوز أن يكون تعالى أضافها إلى اسمه الشريف على سبيل التعظيم لها والتشريف

rows.speaker: الحسن
rows.claim: Ḥasan says peace never ceases among the people of Paradise and is their greeting.
rows.anchor: قال الحسن: إن السلام لا ينقطع عن أهل الجنة وهو تحيتهم

rows.speaker: قتادة
rows.claim: Qatāda says it is reported that the Torah invites the seeker of good forward and tells the seeker of evil to stop.
rows.anchor: وقال قتادة: ذكر لنا أن في التوراة مكتوبا يا باغي الخير هلم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The divine call is general, while guidance is specifically given to whomever God wills; al-Zamakhsharī explains this as granting success where divine kindness will help, in accord with wisdom.
rows.anchor: ولما كان الدعاء عاما لم تتقيد بالمشيئة، ولما كانت الهداية خاصة تقيدت بالمشيئة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Rahq can mean covering or overtaking, and irhāq may mean burdening beyond capacity or approaching; the hadith idiom uses the latter sense.
rows.anchor: وفي الحديث: «أرهقوا القبلة» أي ادنوا منها

rows.speaker: ابن عرفة
rows.claim: Ibn ʿArafa glosses qatar as dust; al-Farazdaq’s verse uses it for the dust over an army, while Ibn Baḥr derives it from fire smoke.
rows.anchor: القتر والقترة الغبار الذي معه سواد، وقال ابن عرفة: الغبار

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: With a still tāʾ, qatr can mean affairs or matters, plural shuʾūn; its original hamz conveys purpose or intent.
rows.anchor: ويقال: القتر بسكون التاء الشأن والأمر، وجمعه شؤون

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Yaʿzubu means to disappear until hidden; related ʿāzib describes something or someone far from home and eventually a man without a wife.
rows.anchor: عزب يعزب ويعزب بكسر الزاي وضمها غاب حتى خفي

rows.speaker: أبو تمام
rows.claim: Abū Tammām’s line uses ʿāzib for a distant meadow, illustrating the sense of something remote.
rows.anchor: وقلقل نأي من خراسان جأشها ... فقلت اطمئني أنضر الروض عازبه

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAbbās says those who do good are those who affirm that there is no deity but God.
rows.anchor: أحسنوا قال ابن عباس: ذكروا كلمة لا إله إلا الله

rows.speaker: الأصم
rows.claim: Al-Aṣamm defines doing good as performing commanded worship properly and avoiding what is prohibited.
rows.anchor: وقال الأصم: أحسنوا في كل ما تعبدوا به

rows.speaker: قيل
rows.claim: Another explanation takes doing good as treating other people well.
rows.anchor: وقيل: أحسنوا معاملة الناس

rows.speaker: أنس
rows.claim: Anas reports the Prophet’s encouragement to do good deeds in worldly life.
rows.anchor: وروى أنس عن رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم: «أحسنوا العمل في الدنيا»

rows.speaker: رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم
rows.claim: In the sound hadith, the Prophet defines ihsan as worshipping God as though one sees Him, or knowing that He sees the worshipper.
rows.anchor: وفي الصحيح: «ما الإحسان؟ قال: أن تعبد الله كأنك تراه

rows.speaker: عيسى عليه السلام
rows.claim: Jesus says that kindness is not merely repaying kindness, but doing good to someone who has acted badly toward you.
rows.anchor: وعن عيسى عليه السلام: ليس الإحسان أن تحسن إلى من أحسن إليك

rows.speaker: الأكثرون
rows.claim: Most interpreters identify al-ḥusnā with Paradise; the report from the Prophet would settle the matter if sound, while al-Ṭabarī favors the broader meaning of every good promised by God.
rows.anchor: والحسنى قال الأكثرون: هي الجنة، وروي ذلك عن الرسول صلى الله عليه وسلم

rows.speaker: الطبري
rows.claim: Al-Ṭabarī reads al-ḥusnā broadly as every good, including all interpretations and promises, and notes that identifying it narrowly as Paradise would repeat the following phrase “people of the Garden.”
rows.anchor: وقال الطبري: الحسنى عام في كل حسن، فهو يعم جميع ما قيل

rows.speaker: عبد الرحمن بن سابط
rows.claim: ʿAbd al-Raḥmān b. Sābiṭ says al-ḥusnā means radiance.
rows.anchor: وقال عبد الرحمن بن سابط: هي النضرة

rows.speaker: ابن زيد
rows.claim: Ibn Zayd says al-ḥusnā is the recompense in the afterlife.
rows.anchor: وقال ابن زيد: الجزاء في الآخرة

rows.speaker: ابن الأنباري
rows.claim: Ibn al-Anbārī is cited for the interpretation of al-ḥusnā as a wish or aspiration.
rows.anchor: وقيل: الأمنية ذكره ابن الأنباري

rows.speaker: الزمخشري
rows.claim: Al-Zamakhsharī reads the increase as bounty beyond the best reward, supported by God’s promise to add from His grace.
rows.anchor: وقال الزمخشري: المثوبة الحسنى وزيادة، وما يزيد على المثوبة وهو التفضل

rows.speaker: علي
rows.claim: ʿAlī interprets the increase as a chamber made from a single pearl.
rows.anchor: وعن علي: الزيادة غرفة من لؤلؤة واحدة

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAbbās interprets the increase as multiplying a good deed tenfold.
rows.anchor: وعن ابن عباس: الحسنى الحسنة والزيادة عشرة أمثالها

rows.speaker: الحسن
rows.claim: Al-Ḥasan says a good deed is multiplied from ten up to seven hundred times.
rows.anchor: وعن الحسن: عشرة أمثالها إلى سبعمائة ضعف

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The segment continues Mujāhid’s interpretation that the increase is God’s forgiveness and approval.
rows.anchor: الزيادة مغفرة من الله ورضوان. وعن زياد بن شجرة

rows.speaker: زياد بن شجرة
rows.claim: Ziyād b. Shajara says a cloud asks the people of Paradise what they want it to rain; whatever they request is sent down.
rows.anchor: وعن زياد بن شجرة: الزيادة أن تمر السحابة بأهل الجنة

rows.speaker: الزمخشري
rows.claim: Al-Zamakhsharī attributes to anthropomorphists and determinists the view that the increase is seeing God, but calls their supporting hadith fabricated.
rows.anchor: وزعمت المشبهة والمجبرة أن الزيادة النظر إلى وجه الله تعالى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Abū Ḥayyān rejects the charge that the vision report is fabricated: Muslim and al-Nasāʾī transmit it from Ṣuhayb from the Prophet, and Ibn al-Mubārak transmits it from Abū Mūsā.
rows.anchor: وأما قوله: وجاءت بحديث موضوع فليس بموضوع، بل خرجه مسلم في صحيحه عن صهيب

rows.speaker: أبو بكر الصديق وعلي بن أبي طالب وحذيفة وعبادة بن الصامت وكعب بن عجرة وأبو موسى وصهيب وابن عباس
rows.claim: Abū Ḥayyān lists these Companions, with qualifications for some reports, and a group of Successors as holding that the increase is seeing God; he says the question belongs to theology.
rows.anchor: وقال: بأن الزيادة هي النظر إلى الله تعالى، أبو بكر الصديق، وعلي بن أبي طالب

rows.speaker: مجاهد
rows.claim: Mujāhid explains that no disgrace overtakes the benefactors, since shame changes and darkens the face.
rows.anchor: قال مجاهد: أراد ولا يلحقها خزي، والخزي يتغير به الوجه

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAbbās interprets the absence of humiliation as freedom from gloom; other views gloss it as disgrace or disappointment.
rows.anchor: قال ابن ابن عباس: والذلة الكآبة. وقال غيره: الهوان.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “Faces” stands for the whole person because it is the noblest part and displays joy and grief; the saved are spared what afflicts the wicked and the faces described in another passage.
rows.anchor: وكنى بالوجه عن الجملة لكونه أشرفها، ولظهور أثر السرر والحزن فيه

rows.speaker: الحسن وأبو رجاء وعيسى بن عمر والأعمش
rows.claim: These readers pronounce qatar with a still tāʾ, a dialect variant like qadar/qadr.
rows.anchor: وقرأ الحسن، وأبو رجاء، وعيسى بن عمر، والأعمش: قتر بسكون التاء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Garden’s people are called its owners because they can dispose of it as owners do, according to their choice.
rows.anchor: وجعلوا أصحاب الجنة لتصرفهم فيها كما يتصرف الملاك

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The passage contrasts those who do good and those who earn sins; the wording distinguishes people who preserve their created disposition through good from those who leave it and acquire evil.
rows.anchor: وجاءت صلة المؤمنين أحسنوا، وصلة الكافرين كسبوا السيئات، تنبيها على أن المؤمن

rows.speaker: قيل
rows.claim: Another parse treats the bāʾ as non-augmentative and supplies an estimated or understood predicate after it.
rows.anchor: وقيل: ليست بزائدة، والتقدير: مقدر بمثلها أو مستقر بمثلها

rows.speaker: الحوفي
rows.claim: Al-Ḥūfī supplies “for them” before the recompense, matching the preceding promise to those who do good; Abū al-Baqāʾ instead supplies “occurring.”
rows.anchor: فقدره الحوفي: لهم جزاء سيئة قال: ودل على تقدير لهم قوله: للذين أحسنوا الحسنى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Grammarians offer several predicates for “those who earned sins”: the recompense clause, “they have no protector,” the image of faces covered by darkness, or “those are the people of the Fire.” Abū Ḥayyān rejects analyses requiring three or four parenthetical clauses.
rows.anchor: الثاني: أن الخبر قوله: ما لهم من الله من عاصم

rows.speaker: ابن عطية
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAṭiyya attaches “those who earned sins” to the preceding “those who did good,” supplying a dropped preposition so each half has a parallel recompense clause.
rows.anchor: وأجاز ابن عطية أن يكون الذين في موضع جر عطفا على قوله

rows.speaker: الأخفش والجمهور
rows.claim: Al-Akhfash explains the construction as coordination over two governing words; most grammarians instead say a preposition was omitted, a disputed grammatical issue.
rows.anchor: فخرجه الأخفش على أنه من العطف على عاملين. وخرجه الجمهور

rows.speaker: ابن عطية
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAṭiyya says the sins include both unbelief and other disobedience: unbelief merits abiding in Hell, while other sins are subject to God’s will.
rows.anchor: ولهذا قال ابن عطية: وتعم السيئات هاهنا الكفر والمعاصي

rows.speaker: الزمخشري
rows.claim: Al-Zamakhsharī argues that equal punishment shows justice, while the increase promised as reward shows divine bounty.
rows.anchor: قال الزمخشري: وفي هذا دليل على أن المراد بالزيادة الفضل

rows.speaker: قيل
rows.claim: Another explanation says punishment is proportionate to the deserved penalty; Hell therefore has levels, with hypocrites in its lowest level.
rows.anchor: وقيل: معنى بمثلها أي: بما يليق بها من العقوبات

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The masculine reading is possible because the feminine noun is non-human; this reverses the saved faces’ freedom from humiliation and dust and stresses the sinners’ blackened faces.
rows.anchor: لأن تأنيث الذلة مجاز، وفي وصف المنافقين نفي القتر والذلة عن وجوههم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The darkened faces are literal discoloration, not metaphor; their blackness is like pieces of night at its deepest darkness, and “from God” can mean from His wrath or from His side.
rows.anchor: وكون وجوههم مسودة هي حقيقة لا مجاز

rows.speaker: أبو عبد الله الرازي
rows.claim: Al-Rāzī transmits philosophers’ allegorical reading: facial darkness signifies ignorance and misguidance, while illuminated faces signify knowledge and joy.
rows.anchor: قال أبو عبد الله الرازي: واعلم أن حكماء الإسلام قالوا: المراد من هذا السواد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Abū Ḥayyān rejects calling Muslim-era philosophers sages, portraying them as enemies of prophets who corrupt Islamic law; he argues their texts are more objectionable than the Torah, whose reading ʿUmar discouraged.
rows.anchor: وهم أحق بأن يسموا سفهاء جهلاء من أن يسموا حكماء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: He condemns the contemporary vogue for philosophy: its adherents call it wisdom, disparage those without it, and neglect memorizing Qurʾān and Prophetic reports.
rows.anchor: وقد غلب في هذا الزمان وقبله بقليل الاشتغال بجهالات الفلاسفة على أكثر الناس

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Abū Ḥayyān recounts that Ibn Rushd’s esteem for philosophers led Andalusian scholars to provoke the Almohad ruler al-Manṣūr into publicly beating, cursing, and humiliating him and a group of associates.
rows.anchor: أغرى به علماء الإسلام بالأندلس المنصور منصور الموحدين يعقوب بن يوسف

rows.speaker: شاعر من العلماء
rows.claim: The poems praise al-Manṣūr for defending Islam and urge him to fight those who abandoned religious law for ancient philosophy and to burn their books.
rows.anchor: فجاهد في أناس قد أضلوا ... طريق الشرع بالعلم القديم

rows.speaker: شاعر
rows.claim: A poem laments a group absorbed in folly who abandoned the religion of guidance while claiming philosophy and wisdom.
rows.anchor: يا وحشة الإسلام من فرقة ... شاغلة أنفسها بالسفه

rows.speaker: شاعر
rows.claim: Another poem says the new group follows Ibn Sīnā or Abū Naṣr in religion.
rows.anchor: لا تقتدي في الدين إلا بما ... سن ابن سينا أو أبو نصر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Abū Ḥayyān contrasts Egypt, where philosophy was studied openly without objection, with al-Andalus, where logic books were sold secretly and the subject was euphemistically called al-mifaʿl.
rows.anchor: إذ كنا نشأنا في جزيرة الأندلس على التبرؤ من ذلك والإنكار له

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: His friend, the minister Ibn al-Ḥakīm, asked him to acquire a logic book but used the euphemism al-mifaʿl even in his letter.
rows.anchor: فسماه في كتابه لي بالمفعل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Night imagery intensifies blackness because darkness reaches its deepest point at night, following the mention of faces being covered.
rows.anchor: ولما كانت ظلمة الليل نهاية في السواد شبه سواد وجوههم بقطع من الليل

rows.speaker: ابن كثير والكسائي
rows.claim: Ibn Kathīr and al-Kisāʾī read qiṭʿ with a still ṭāʾ, a singular noun meaning something cut off; al-Akhfash glosses it as the blackness of night.
rows.anchor: وقرأ ابن كثير والكسائي قطعا بسكون الطاء، وهو مفرد اسم للشيء المقطوع

rows.speaker: ابن أبي عبلة
rows.claim: Ibn Abī ʿAbla has the same reading of qiṭʿ as the preceding readers, but with a fatḥa on ṭāʾ.
rows.anchor: أبي عبلة كذلك إلا أنه فتح الطاء

rows.speaker: قيل
rows.claim: Another parse takes qiṭaʿ as the plural of qiṭʿa; it can then take masculine or feminine agreement, and mudhliman may describe the night or the pieces themselves.
rows.anchor: وقيل: قطع جمع قطعة، نحو سدر وسدرة، فيجوز إذ ذاك

rows.speaker: الزمخشري
rows.claim: Al-Zamakhsharī proposes that mudhliman is circumstantial from “night,” governed either by aghshiyat or by the verbal meaning of min al-layl.
rows.anchor: قال الزمخشري: (فإن قلت) : إذا جعلت مظلما حالا من الليل، فما العامل فيه؟

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Abū Ḥayyān finds the first governing analysis remote because the modifier and its noun have different governors; he prefers understanding the patches as belonging to the night in its darkness.
rows.anchor: أما الوجه الأول فهو بعيد، لأن الأصل أن يكون العامل في الحال هو العامل

rows.speaker: ابن عطية
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAṭiyya notes that if mudhliman modifies qiṭʿ it follows the clause rather than precedes it, and supplies an implied “settled”; Abū Ḥayyān says an active participle needs no such verbal clause.
rows.anchor: قال ابن عطية: فإذا كان نعتا يعني: مظلما نعتا لقطع، فكان حقه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The pronoun in “We gather them” refers back to both those who did good and those who earned sins; another view limits it to sinners, including idolaters and people who worship nothing.
rows.anchor: الضمير في نحشرهم عائد على من تقدم ذكرهم من الذين أحسنوا

rows.speaker: الحسن وشيبة والقراء السبعة
rows.claim: Ḥasan, Shayba, and the seven readers recite nahshuruhum with first-person plural; another group reads yahshuruhum in the third person.
rows.anchor: وقرأ الحسن وشيبة والقراء السبعة: نحشرهم بالنون، وقرأت فرقة بالياء

rows.speaker: الزمخشري
rows.claim: Al-Zamakhsharī paraphrases makānakum as “remain in your place; do not leave until you see what happens to you.”
rows.anchor: وعلى الأول عول الزمخشري فقال: مكانكم الزموا مكانكم لا تبرحوا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The apparent parse makes antum emphasize the implicit subject of the command noun, with the partners coordinated to that subject.
rows.anchor: فالظاهر ما ذكرناه من أنه تأكيد للضمير المستكن في مكانكم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Abū Ḥayyān rejects deriving the command noun from alzimū: makānakum cannot take an object, whereas alzimū is transitive, and command-nouns retain their verbs’ transitivity.
rows.anchor: إذ لو كان كذلك لكان مكانك الذي هو اسم فعل يتعدى كما يتعدى الزموا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The partners are variously identified as devils, angels, idols, or any being worshipped besides God; if idols, God gives them speech to deny the expected intercession.
rows.anchor: حال، والشركاء الشياطين أو الملائكة أو الأصنام أو من عبد من دون الله

rows.speaker: رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم
rows.claim: A report says that when unbelievers see punishment, they are told to follow what they worshipped; they claim to have worshipped the partners, who disown them.
rows.anchor: وروي عن النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم: «أن الكفار إذا رأوا العذاب

rows.speaker: ابن عطية
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAṭiyya says the exchange seems to concern idols, not angels or Jesus, nor Pharaoh or jinn, since those beings were aware of their worship.
rows.anchor: قال ابن عطية: فظاهر هذه الآية أن محاورتهم إنما هي مع الأصنام دون الملائكة وعيسى ابن مريم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Makānakum is an imperative noun meaning “stay” or “remain”; grammarians dispute whether such nouns have a syntactic case position.
rows.anchor: ومكانكم عده النحويون في أسماء الأفعال

rows.speaker: ابن عطية
rows.claim: Abū Ḥayyān rejects making antum emphasize an omitted verb such as “halt”: emphasis cannot follow a command noun that bears no pronoun, and an omitted emphasized expression is not idiomatic.
rows.anchor: وهذا ليس بجيد، إذ لو كان تأكيدا لذلك الضمير المتصل بالفعل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Wāḥidī defines tazyīl, tazayyul, and muzāyala as distinction and parting; Abū Ḥayyān paraphrases the verse as separating their worldly bonds.
rows.anchor: فزيلنا ففرقنا بينهم وقطعنا أقرانهم

rows.speaker: ابن قتيبة وأبو البقاء
rows.claim: Abū Ḥayyān rejects Ibn Qutayba’s derivation of zayyalnā from zāla/yazūlu, adopted by Abū al-Baqāʾ; the form and verbal noun instead support the root with yāʾ.
rows.anchor: وزعم ابن قتيبة أن زيلنا من مادة زال يزول، وتبعه أبو البقاء.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Fa-zayyalnā means God separated the partners and worshippers, severing their worldly bonds or distancing them after gathering them together at the assembly.
rows.anchor: فزيلنا ففرقنا بينهم وقطعنا أقرانهم

rows.speaker: الفراء
rows.claim: Al-Farrāʾ reports the variant fa-zāyalnā, which al-Zamakhsharī compares with other forms where fāʿala and faʿala share a sense.
rows.anchor: وقرأت فرقة: فزايلنا حكاه الفراء

rows.speaker: الحوفي
rows.claim: Al-Ḥūfī supplies an omitted verb, “stay” or “remain,” for makānakum.
rows.anchor: قال الحوفي: مكانكم نصب بإضمار فعل أي: الزموا مكانكم أو اثبتوا.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Abū Ḥayyān rejects Ibn ʿAṭiyya’s parse that makes antum a new subject with an omitted predicate, since it breaks the connected clause and requires needless ellipsis.
rows.anchor: وهذا ضعيف لفك الكلام الظاهر اتصال بعض أجزائه ببعض

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The apparent meaning of tazyīl is bodily separation and distance between partners and worshippers, after they had been assembled; an alternate account makes the division one of argument and belief.
rows.anchor: والظاهر أن التزييل أو المزايلة هو بمفارقة الأجسام وتباعده

rows.speaker: ابن عطية
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAṭiyya says the separation may instead be in argument and belief; Abū Ḥayyān favors actual bodily separation.
rows.anchor: وقيل: فرقنا بينهم في الحجة والمذهب قاله ابن عطية

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Past-form verbs are coordinated with a future and carry future meaning; the partners’ denial refutes the worshippers’ claim, and they call God as witness when dispute begins.
rows.anchor: ونفي الشركاء عبادة المشركين هو رد لقولهم: لإياكم كنا نعبد، والمعنى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Shahīdan is more convincingly parsed as specification because it accepts min, rather than as a circumstantial accusative; inna is read as either a reduced emphatic or a negative with illā meaning “only.”
rows.anchor: وانتصب شهيدا، قيل: على الحال، والأصح على التمييز لقبوله من

rows.speaker: ابن عطية
rows.claim: The partners’ claim that they were unaware favors idols: inert images cannot perceive worship, unlike rational beings such as humans, jinn, or angels.
rows.anchor: وهذا يرجح أن الشركاء هي الأصنام كما قال ابن عطية

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Hunālika denotes the bewildering assembly or, by borrowing a place adverb for time, that moment; each soul then encounters what it sent ahead.
rows.anchor: هنالك ظرف مكان أي: في ذلك الموقف والمقام المقتضي للحيرة

rows.speaker: السدي
rows.claim: Al-Suddī reads tatlu as “follow and seek” the deeds sent ahead, citing a poem about one suspect following another.
rows.anchor: تتبع وتطلب ما أسلفت من أعمالها، قاله السدي

rows.speaker: قيل
rows.claim: The reading tatlu may instead mean reading the books handed to each soul.
rows.anchor: قيل: ويصح أن يكون من التلاوة وهي القراءة

rows.speaker: قراء السبعة
rows.claim: The seven readers’ tablu means each soul tests and recognizes its past deeds as ugly or good, harmful or beneficial, accepted or rejected; ʿĀṣim has nablū, “We test.”
rows.anchor: وقرأ باقي السبعة: تبلوا بالتاء والباء أي: تختبر ما أسلفت من العمل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: On the nablū reading, kull nafs is the object and mā aslafat may be its apposition or an object after an omitted preposition.
rows.anchor: وكل نفس بالنصب، وما أسلفت بدل من كل نفس

rows.speaker: الحسن والكلبي
rows.claim: Ḥasan reads the verb as receiving; al-Kalbī says knowing, and another gloss is tasting. The nablū reading may also mean God afflicts each sinful soul for its evil deeds.
rows.anchor: وعن الحسن تبلوا تتسلم. وعن الكلبي: تعلم. وقيل: تذوق.

rows.speaker: يحيى بن وثاب
rows.claim: Yaḥyā b. Waththāb reads ruddu with kasra on rāʾ, transferred from dāl when its vowel is removed in assimilation.
rows.anchor: وقرأ يحيى بن وثاب: وردوا بكسر الراء، لما سكن للإدغام

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Returning to God means returning to His punishment or the place of recompense; He is their true master in ownership and encompassing authority, not aid or mercy.
rows.anchor: ومعنى إلى الله: إلى عقابه. وقيل: إلى موضع جزائه مولاهم الحق

rows.speaker: الزمخشري
rows.claim: Al-Zamakhsharī takes al-ḥaqq in the accusative as an expression of praise, or as emphasizing that they return to God rather than false idols.
rows.anchor: وقرىء الحق بالنصب على المدح نحو: الحمد لله أهل الحمد

rows.speaker: أبو عبد الله الرازي
rows.claim: Al-Rāzī says they are forced to acknowledge God’s divinity after worshipping others, which explains calling Him their true master.
rows.anchor: وقال أبو عبد الله الرازي: وردوا إلى الله، جعلوا ملجأين إلى الإقرار بالإلهية

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: What they falsely claimed about idols as God’s partners and intercessors vanishes and proves empty.
rows.anchor: وضل عنهم أي: بطل وذهب ما كانوا يفترونه من الكذب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: After exposing idol worship, God confronts them with undeniable evidence: provision, hearing and sight, life and death, and governance of all things.
rows.anchor: لما بين فضائح عبدة الأوثان، أتبعها بذكر الدلائل على فساد مذهبهم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Provision essential to life comes from rain in the sky and vegetation on earth; min marks its source and indicates generosity from both upper and lower worlds.
rows.anchor: فمن السماء بالمطر، ومن الأرض بالنبات

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Hearing and sight are the two noblest senses: hearing enables perception, sight surveys creation, and God controls their preservation or removal.
rows.anchor: ثم ذكر ملكه لهاتين الحاستين الشريفتين: السمع الذي هو سبب مدارك الأشياء

rows.speaker: الزمخشري
rows.claim: Al-Zamakhsharī explains God’s control as creating the senses in their remarkable form or protecting them from pervasive injury; Abū Ḥayyān says these nuances do not follow from the wording.
rows.anchor: وقال الزمخشري: من يملك السمع والأبصار من يستطيع خلقهما وتسويتهما

rows.speaker: علي
rows.claim: ʿAlī praises God as one who gives sight through fat, hearing through bone, and speech through flesh.
rows.anchor: وعن علي كرم الله وجهه: سبحان من بصر بشحم، وأسمع بعظم، وأنطق بلحم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Here am signals transition to another proof rather than abrogating the prior question with bal; it cannot be treated as bal without the interrogative hamza.
rows.anchor: وأم هنا تقتضي تقدير بل دون همزة الاستفهام

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Hearing and sight stand for the senses generally because they are most distinguished; creating living from dead and dead from living displays God’s power to bring opposites from one another.
rows.anchor: ونبه تعالى بالسمع والبصر على الحواس لأنهما أشرفها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The universal statement that God governs all things follows four examples because His governance has no limit; the unbelievers cannot deny that God provides, controls, creates life and death, and governs.
rows.anchor: ومن يدبر الأمر شامل لما تقدم من الأشياء الأربعة المذكورة ولغيرها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “Will you not be mindful?” warns them to fear punishment for inventing partners for God; alternatively it asks them to take warning and stop.
rows.anchor: ومعنى أفلا تتقون: أفلا تخافون عقوبة الله في افترائكم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “That is God, your true Lord” points to the one possessing the preceding attributes, whose exclusive divinity merits worship, unlike false idols.
rows.anchor: فذلكم إشارة إلى من اختص بالأوصاف السابقة، الحق الثابت الربوبية

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “What is beyond truth except error?” functions as a negative assertion and rebuke; truth and error have no middle ground because they are opposites.
rows.anchor: وماذا استفهام معناه النفي، ولذلك دخلت إلا، وصحبه التقرير والتوبيخ

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Grammatically, mā and dhā can combine as one interrogative “what,” with “after truth” as predicate; alternatively dhā is relative and its clause predicates mā.
rows.anchor: وماذا مبتدأ تركبت ذا مع ما فصار مجموعهما استفهاما

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Since God alone has just been shown to possess those attributes, the rebuke asks how people can turn from manifest truth and worship beings sharing none of them.
rows.anchor: ثم وبخهم على اتباع الضلال بعد وضوح الحق قال تعالى: فأنى تصرفون

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Using this verse to prove that chess is error is unconvincing: the passage concerns belief, unbelief, and worship, not subsidiary practices on which laws and jurists differ.
rows.anchor: واستنباط كون الشطرنج ضلالا من قوله: فماذا بعد الحق إلا الضلال

rows.speaker: الجبائي
rows.claim: Al-Jubbāʾī uses “how are you turned?” against determinists: if God turns unbelievers from belief they should not be blamed, just as a blind person does not say they blinded themself.
rows.anchor: وقد تعلق الجبائي بهذه الآية في الرد على المجبرة

rows.speaker: الزمخشري
rows.claim: Al-Zamakhsharī connects the decree to the preceding contrast between truth and error or to their being turned away; Ibn ʿAṭiyya compares it with God’s attributes and the people’s chosen course.
rows.anchor: قال الزمخشري: كذلك مثل ذلك الحق حقت كلمة ربك

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The comparative kāf is accusative in function; “thus” can refer to their turning after recognizing truth or to the truth itself.
rows.anchor: كذلك الكاف للتشبيه في موضع نصب، والإشارة بذلك قيل: إلى المصدر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Fusuq means persisting in unbelief to its furthest limit; “they do not believe” either apposes God’s word or explains a decree of punishment as caused by unbelief.
rows.anchor: ومعنى فسقوا: تمردوا في كفرهم وخرجوا إلى الحد الأقصى فيه

rows.speaker: ابن أبي عبلة
rows.claim: Ibn Abī ʿAbla reads inna with kasra, supporting the interpretation “because they do not believe.”
rows.anchor: ويوضح هذا الوجه قراءة ابن أبي عبلة: إنهم لا يؤمنون بالكسر

rows.speaker: قراء السبعة وأبو جعفر وشيبة والصاحبان
rows.claim: Abū Jaʿfar, Shayba, and the two Basran readers have plural kalimāt here and at the sūra’s end; the other readers use singular kalimat.
rows.anchor: وقرأ أبو جعفر وشيبة والصاحبان: كلمات على الجمع هنا وفي آخر السورة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The question about originating and restoring creation establishes that these are grounds for worship; unbelievers accept the first but deny the second despite a clear rational proof and the revealed obligation to believe it.
rows.anchor: إذ هو من الواضحات التي لا يختلف في إمكانها العقلاء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Prophet’s answer states subject and predicate in a complete sentence, reinforcing the proof; the earlier answer “God” needed no repeated predicate because they could not deny it.
rows.anchor: وأبرز الجواب في جملة مبتدأة مصرح بخبرها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Tuʾfakūn means that they are turned away or turned around from following the truth.
rows.anchor: ومعنى تؤفكون تصرفون وتقلبون عن اتباع الحق

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: After showing idols cannot create or resurrect, the argument shows they cannot guide to truth; creation and guidance recur together as evidence for the Creator, including the accounts of Moses and God’s creation and guidance of all things.
rows.anchor: وقد أعقب الخلق بالهداية في القرآن في مواضع قال تعالى حكاية عن الكليم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Human minds can err, so only God guides them; lifeless idols have no effect, and anything alive is itself guided by God rather than capable of directing others.
rows.anchor: ولما كانت العقول يلحقها الاضطراب والغلط، بين تعالى أنه لا يهديهما إلا هو

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Hadā is transitive to two objects, with its second introduced by ilā or li; in “guides to truth,” the first object is omitted, and the verb cannot mean “find the way” because the parallel is transitive.
rows.anchor: وهدى تتعدى بنفسها إلى اثنين، وإلى الثاني بإلى وباللام

rows.speaker: المبرد
rows.claim: Al-Mubarrad rejects al-Kisāʾī, al-Farrāʾ, and al-Zamakhsharī’s use of hadā to mean ihtadā, saying the language does not support it.
rows.anchor: وقد أنكر المبرد ما قاله الكسائي والفراء وتبعهما الزمخشري

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Aḥaqq is not a comparative adjective here; it means that God is entitled to be followed.
rows.anchor: وأحق ليست أفعل تفضيل، بل المعنى حقيق بأن يتبع

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Since idolaters believe their partners guide, the Prophet is told to answer directly that God guides to truth; the separated am construction is described as the more eloquent pattern.
rows.anchor: أمر نبيه صلى الله عليه وسلم بأن يبادر بالجواب فقال: قل الله يهدي للحق

rows.speaker: أهل المدينة إلا ورشا
rows.claim: The Medinan readers other than Warsh pronounce yahdi with fatḥa on yāʾ, a still hāʾ, and doubled dāl; grammarians describe a slight vowel to break the two-sukūn sequence.
rows.anchor: وقرأ أهل المدينة إلا ورشا: أمن لا يهدي بفتح الياء وسكون الهاء

rows.speaker: أبو عمرو وقالون
rows.claim: Abū ʿAmr and Qālūn have the same form but lightly articulate the vowel, which Sībawayh calls ikhtilās.
rows.anchor: وقرأ أبو عمرو وقالون في رواية كذلك: إلا أنه اختلس الحركة

rows.speaker: ابن عامر وابن كثير وورش وابن محيصن
rows.claim: These readers open the hāʾ in the form derived from yahtadī, transferring the tāʾ’s vowel to hāʾ and assimilating tāʾ into dāl.
rows.anchor: وقرأ ابن عامر، وابن كثير، وورش، وابن محيصن: كذلك إلا أنهم فتحوا الهاء

rows.speaker: حفص ويعقوب والأعمش عن أبي بكر
rows.claim: These readers use kasra on hāʾ to supply the needed vowel; Abū Ḥātim calls this a dialect of lower Muḍar.
rows.anchor: وقرأ حفص، ويعقوب، والأعمش عن أبي بكر كذلك، إلا أنهم كسروا الهاء

rows.speaker: أبو بكر في رواية يحيى بن آدم
rows.claim: Abū Bakr, in Yaḥyā b. Ādam’s narration, additionally has kasra on yāʾ.
rows.anchor: وقرأ أبو بكر في رواية يحيى بن آدم كذلك، إلا أنه كسر الياء

rows.speaker: سيبويه
rows.claim: Sībawayh disallows yahdi because kasra on yāʾ is heavy, though he allows tahdi, nahdi, and ahdi.
rows.anchor: ونقل عن سيبويه أنه لا يجيز يهدي، ويجيز تهدي ونهدي وأهدي

rows.speaker: حمزة والكسائي وخلف ويحيى بن وثاب والأعمش
rows.claim: These readers use yahdī, the present tense of hadā; al-Zamakhsharī interprets the contrast as God’s guiding compared with an idol unable to guide unless guided.
rows.anchor: وقرأ حمزة، والكسائي، وخلف، ويحيى بن وثاب، والأعمش: يهدي مضارع هدى

rows.speaker: أبو علي الفارسي
rows.claim: Abū ʿAlī al-Fārisī says idols cannot find their way even if guided; describing them with rational predicates is figurative language applied to worshipped beings.
rows.anchor: وقال أبو علي الفارسي: وصف الأصنام بأنها لا تهتدي إلا أن تهدى

rows.speaker: ابن عطية
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAṭiyya says the Hamza-Kisāʾī reading may mean that no one guides others except through God’s guidance; other readings fit the figurative account of idols unable to guide themselves.
rows.anchor: وقال ابن عطية: والذي أقول إن قراءة حمزة والكسائي يحتمل أن يكون المعنى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The idols’ glorification of God may itself be their guidance; alternatively, the clause can end at “does not guide,” with a detached exception meaning the idol needs guidance, or describe misleading leaders who can be guided.
rows.anchor: ويحتمل أن يكون ما ذكر الله من تسبيح الجمادات هو اهتداؤها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “What is wrong with you?” expresses astonishment at worshipping beings unable to guide even themselves; “How do you judge?” separately condemns equating idols with the Lord of all worlds.
rows.anchor: فما لكم استفهام معناه التعجب والإنكار أي: أي شيء لكم في اتخاذ هؤلاء الشركاء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Most people follow conjecture about God and His attributes without proof, passing beliefs along from their ancestors; some interpret “most” as all, or specifically refer to beliefs about idols and their intercession.
rows.anchor: الظاهر أن أكثرهم على بابه، لأن منهم من تبصر في الأصنام ورفضها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Conjecture cannot deliver knowledge of truth because it remains possibility rather than certainty; the verse warns against unreasoned speculation and imitation of forebears.
rows.anchor: والظن في معرفة الله لا يغني من الحق شيئا أي: من إدراك الحق

rows.speaker: عبد الله
rows.claim: ʿAbd Allāh reads the closing verb in the second person, shifting to direct address and intensifying the warning.
rows.anchor: وقرأ عبد الله: تفعلون بالتاء على الخطاب التفاتا

rows.speaker: قيل
rows.claim: One report says the passage was revealed about the leaders of the Jews and Quraysh.
rows.anchor: وقيل: نزلت في رؤساء اليهود وقريش

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: In response to demands for another Qurʾān and accusations of fabrication, God says it is impossible or improper for this miraculous, comprehensive revelation to have been invented.
rows.anchor: لما تقدم قولهم: ائت بقرآن غير هذا أو بدله

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The demonstrative “this” magnifies the Qurʾān and points to its qualities that make fabrication impossible; the clearest grammar makes an yuftara the predicate of kāna.
rows.anchor: والإشارة بهذا فيها تفخيم المشار إليه وتعظيمه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Abū Ḥayyān rejects the claim that an replaces a deleted lām in the lām of denial: there is no evidence the particles alternate; otherwise an yuftara would not itself be the predicate.
rows.anchor: والصحيح أنهما لا يتعاقبان، وأنه لا يجوز حذف اللام وإظهار أن

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: The revelation “before it” means earlier divine scriptures, as Ibn ʿAbbās explains from “confirming what is with you.”
rows.anchor: والذي بين يديه الكتب الإلهية المتقدمة قاله ابن عباس

rows.speaker: الزجاج
rows.claim: Al-Zajjāj suggests that “what is before it” means signs of the Hour; Abū Ḥayyān rejects this because Quraysh had not witnessed them, whereas agreement with Torah and Gospel is evidence despite the Prophet’s lack of access to them.
rows.anchor: وعن الزجاج الذي بين يديه أشراط الساعة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Tafṣīl al-kitāb means explaining the commands, rulings, and laws contained in scripture.
rows.anchor: وتفصيل الكتاب تبيين ما فرض وكتب فيه من الأحكام والشرائع

rows.speaker: الكسائي والفراء ومحمد بن سعدان والزجاج
rows.claim: The majority reading has accusative taṣdīqan and tafṣīlan; these grammarians parse them as predicates of an omitted kāna after “but,” meaning the Qurʾān confirms and explains.
rows.anchor: وقرأ الجمهور: تصديق وتفصيل بالنصب، فخرجه الكسائي والفراء ومحمد بن سعدان

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Other parses of the accusatives make them purpose phrases after an omitted verb or cognate objects after an omitted verb.
rows.anchor: وقيل: انتصب مفعولا من أجله، والعامل محذوف

rows.speaker: عيسى بن عمر
rows.claim: ʿĪsā b. ʿUmar reads both “confirmation” and “explanation” in the nominative, supplying an omitted subject pronoun: “but it is confirmation.”
rows.anchor: تفصيل وتصديق بالرفع، وفي يوسف خبر مبتدأ محذوف

rows.speaker: الفراء
rows.claim: Al-Farrāʾ claims conjunction with wāw favors a doubled nūn in lakinna while its absence favors a light nūn; Abū Ḥayyān notes both occur with wāw in canonical readings.
rows.anchor: وزعم الفراء ومن تابعه أن العرب إذا قالت ولكن بالواو آثرت تشديد النون

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “No doubt in it” qualifies the confirmation and explanation: the Qurʾān is free of doubt and comes from the Lord of all worlds.
rows.anchor: ولا ريب فيه داخل في حيز الاستدراك كأنه قيل: ولكن تصديقا وتفصيلا

rows.speaker: الزمخشري
rows.claim: Al-Zamakhsharī allows min rabb al-ʿālamīn to modify confirmation and explanation, with “no doubt in it” as an aside; Abū Ḥayyān says grammatically it can govern only one through shared government.
rows.anchor: قال الزمخشري: ويجوز أن يراد ولكن كان تصديقا من رب العالمين

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: After rejecting fabrication and identifying the Qurʾān as confirmation and explanation, the passage offers inimitability as the strongest proof and recalls the earlier challenge in al-Baqara.
rows.anchor: ذكر أعظم دليل على أنه من عند الله وهو الإعجاز الذي اشتمل عليه

rows.speaker: سيبويه
rows.claim: On Sībawayh’s analysis, am means “rather, do they say?” with an interrogative hamza that reports or condemns the claim.
rows.anchor: على مذهب سيبويه أي: بل أيقولون اختلقه

rows.speaker: فرقة
rows.claim: One group treats am simply as the interrogative hamza.
rows.anchor: وقالت فرقة: أم هذه بمنزلة همزة الاستفهام

rows.speaker: أبو عبيدة
rows.claim: Abū ʿUbayda takes am as wāw, effectively “and they say he fabricated it.”
rows.anchor: وقال أبو عبيدة: أم بمعنى الواو ومجازه

rows.speaker: قيل
rows.claim: Other proposals say the mīm is extra, leaving simply “do they say?”, or make am the counterpart of an omitted preceding question.
rows.anchor: وقيل: الميم صلة، والتقدير أيقولون
